summary: A quiet weekend before a big week: Ontario's fall update shows deeper deficits, Ottawa tables its budget Wednesday, and Toronto's bike-lane fight returns.
body: Ontario's fall economic statement, released on Wednesday, says the trade war with the US has pushed the province's return to a balanced budget back a year, to 2029-30 [^1][^2]. The province now expects deficits of $16.9 billion this year, $12.7 billion next year and $6.7 billion the year after, about $36 billion in total, and it cut its 2026 growth forecast to 0.5% from 1% [^1][^2]. The main new measure is an $8-billion "Ontario Competitiveness Tax Cut" that lets businesses deduct the full cost of new equipment and buildings right away, which the government says could bring $11 billion in investment and up to 30,000 jobs [^1][^2]. There is also a tax break for buyers of newly built homes [^1]. Interest on the province's debt costs about $1.4 billion a month [^1]. Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy says the deficits "are necessary in the current environment" [^2].

Ottawa's turn comes on Wednesday, November 5, when Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne tables the Carney government's second budget [^3]. The government says it is on track to balance its day-to-day (operating) spending by 2027-28, while the Parliamentary Budget Officer projects that goal will be missed by a year [^3]. Ottawa ran a $5.36-billion deficit from April to August [^4]. The budget lands the day after Tuesday's US midterms, where Canada's trade dispute has become a campaign issue [^6]. Prime Minister Mark Carney says any progress in talks is because "the U.S. is coming closer to our position," while officials warn that more talking does not mean a deal is near [^5][^6].

Closer to home, Ontario's transportation minister said on Friday that 1.2 kilometres of bike lanes on Bloor Street West in Etobicoke have been removed, the "first part" of the province's plan to take out lanes on parts of Bloor, Yonge, Avenue Road and around Queen's Park to ease traffic [^7]. Dozens of cyclists protested at Queen's Park on Saturday, and Cycle Toronto has asked the Supreme Court of Canada to hear its challenge [^7]. My read: this week's two budgets will show how governments plan to pay for the trade war, which matters for jobs, housing and tuition support in Ontario.
differences: Ottawa says it will balance its operating budget by 2027-28; the Parliamentary Budget Officer expects that to slip a year [^3]. On trade, a White House adviser has suggested a deal is close, while Carney says he cannot be sure Trump would honour one [^5][^6]. The province says bike-lane removal eases congestion; cycling groups dispute this in court [^7].

reads.summary: The clearest list of what Ontario plans to spend, cut and borrow, and why balance is now four years away.
